918.title: Namdev
918.howItsDone: Varkari devotees in Maharashtra sing Namdev's songs to Vitthal, and Sikhs read and sing the hymns under his name in the Guru Granth Sahib, where his words are kept beside those of the Gurus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Namdev was called half-baked by a potter, and then learned from Visoba Khechar's feet that there's nowhere without God. Did an ordinary place surprise you? Day nine hundred eighteen.

Lunch is laid out: a few pieces of flatbread, and beside them a little pot of ghee, clarified butter, to spread on top. Namdev looks away for a moment. A stray dog trots in, snatches the bread, and runs. Namdev jumps up and goes after it. Not with a stick. He's carrying the pot of ghee, calling after the dog: wait, wait, that bread is dry, let me put some butter on it for you. That's the story told about him. And it only makes sense if you remember yesterday.
screen: `A DOG STEALS THE BREAD.` → `NAMDEV CHASES IT.` → `HE'S CARRYING THE GHEE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Visoba taught Namdev that there's no place without God. Today's story is that lesson trotting off on four legs. Someone who has really learned it can't see a hungry dog as only a thief. In the story, Namdev sees Vitthal in it, and the one problem left is that the bread is dry. Some tellings say Vitthal then shows himself, smiling. Either way, the point lands. Now a second story, and a harder one. Namdev goes to a temple to sing; tradition places it at Aundha. He's singing in front of the shrine when the priests push him out. In their eyes, a man of his birth doesn't belong there. So Namdev walks around to the back of the temple, sits down on the ground, and keeps singing. And the story says the temple turned. The whole building swung around until its door faced Namdev and its back faced the priests. What sets this one apart is that Namdev tells it himself, in a hymn kept under his name in the Guru Granth Sahib, the scripture of the Sikhs. In it, roughly, he says he came to the temple laughing and playing, that he was seized and driven out because of the community he was born into, and that the temple turned to face him. So Namdev's own words sit inside the Sikh scripture, beside the hymns of the Gurus. Put the two stories side by side. In the first, God is so near that even a dog with stolen lunch is him. In the second, God is so near that he won't stay in a building that sends his singer away. Namdev doesn't have to go looking. Both times, God comes around to wherever Namdev already is.
screen: `THE LESSON ON FOUR LEGS.` · `PUSHED OUT OF THE TEMPLE.` · `THE TEMPLE TURNS.` · then, large: `A HYMN IN THE GURU GRANTH SAHIB.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow down. Bring to mind one creature that annoyed you lately: a neighbor's dog, a pigeon on the windowsill, a person who took something that felt like yours, even something small, like a parking spot or the last cup of coffee. Hold them in mind for a moment without the annoyance. Then try Namdev's question: if this one were holy too, what would I hand them? Nothing grand. Just the ghee for the bread. Let the answer stay small and real. If you pray, you can hold that one before God. The bell holds the time.
Namdev. The poet-saint of Pandharpur who chased a dog to butter its bread, and whose hymn of the turning temple is kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.

Your line: the butter, not the stick. Today, when something gets taken from you, a seat, a minute, the last slice, try running after it with the butter instead of the stick. Day nine hundred eighteen.

919.title: Tukaram
919.carry: one for you and one for me
919.howItsDone: Tukaram belongs to the Varkari tradition of Maharashtra; Varkaris sing his songs to Vitthal at home and in temples, and the stories of his life are told and retold among them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Namdev ran after a dog with the butter, and sang behind a temple until, the story says, it turned to face him. What did you hand over instead of grabbing back? Day nine hundred nineteen.

A man is walking home along a village road with an armful of sugarcane, a gift from a farmer whose field he'd been helping with. Sugarcane is a treat: you peel it and chew it for the sweet juice. Children see him coming and run up. Can we have some? He hands one stalk to the first child. Then one to the next, and the next. By the time he reaches his own door, he's holding a single stalk. Waiting inside is his wife, who has a household to feed. The man is Tukaram, and today we meet him.
screen: `AN ARMFUL OF SUGARCANE.` → `THE CHILDREN ASK.` → `ONE STALK LEFT.`

segments.voice: Tukaram is remembered as a grocer in the village of Dehu, on the Indrayani river. He was a devotee of Vitthal, the same god of Pandharpur that Namdev sang to. Tradition even ties the two together: it says Namdev came to Tukaram in a dream, with Vitthal beside him, and set him the task of making songs. And the songs came. But the stories don't pretend his life was easy. Tradition says his shop failed, that famine hit his region, and that he lost people he loved. Out of that grief, the stories say, he turned his whole life toward Vitthal. Which brings us back to the door, and the one stalk. His wife is waiting, and she's furious. Tradition remembers her as sharp-tongued, but the story is fair to her: the family is poor, and her husband keeps giving everything away. She grabs the last stalk and brings it down across his back. It snaps in two. And Tukaram, rubbing his shoulder, looks at the two pieces and says something like: wonderful, now there's one for you and one for me. You can hear it two ways, and both are true to him. It's funny. It's also a man who has decided, all the way down, that nothing he's handed is really his to hoard, not the cane, not even the moment of being hit. The anger doesn't get a fight back. It gets half the sugarcane. The Varkari tradition he belonged to doesn't ask anyone to leave home for a cave. It holds up people like this: a grocer, a husband, with debts and a hungry household waiting at the door, singing to Vitthal right in the middle of it.
screen: `A GROCER OF DEHU.` · `NAMDEV IN A DREAM.` · `THE STALK SNAPS IN TWO.` · then, large: `ONE FOR YOU AND ONE FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Think of one thing you were handed recently that you didn't fully keep: time, money, attention, patience, that you gave away along the road, maybe before it got to the people at home. Don't scold yourself, and don't defend yourself either. Just notice where it went. Then think of the person waiting at your own door. What's the one stalk you could still split with them today? Let it be something small. If you pray, you can hold both the road and the door before God. The bell holds the time.
Tukaram. The grocer-saint of Dehu who gave away the sugarcane on the road home, and split the last broken stalk with the wife who broke it.
Your line: one for you and one for me. Today, when something breaks in an argument, look for the way to say: one for you and one for me. Day nine hundred nineteen.

920.title: Tukaram
920.tomorrow: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
920.howItsDone: Varkaris sing Tukaram's abhangs in kirtan and on the yearly walking pilgrimage to Pandharpur, when a palanquin carrying his sandals travels from Dehu with the pilgrims.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tukaram gave away the sugarcane on the road home, and when the last stalk broke across his back, he split it: one for you, one for me. Did anything get split instead of fought over? Day nine hundred twenty.
screen: `TUKARAM.` · `ONE FOR YOU AND ONE FOR ME.`

segments.voice: On the bank of the Indrayani, a man is holding a bundle of handwritten notebooks, full of songs. He steps to the edge and lets them go. They sink into the brown water and are gone. Nobody stole them. Nobody tore them up. He was told to do this, and he did it himself. Then he sits down on the riverbank, on the bare ground by the water, and he doesn't get up.
screen: `A BUNDLE OF NOTEBOOKS.` → `INTO THE RIVER.` → `HE SITS DOWN ON THE BANK.`

segments.voice: The songs are abhangs, the short devotional verses of the Varkari saints, made to be sung, in Marathi, the everyday language Jnaneshwar had already opened the Gita in. Tukaram had been making them for Vitthal, and people were singing them. Not everyone was pleased. Tradition names a learned man, Rameshwar Bhatt, who objected that a grocer had no business composing songs about sacred things, and in everyday Marathi at that. The story says he ordered Tukaram to sink his notebooks in the river. And Tukaram did. Notice that. He doesn't argue, doesn't hide a copy, doesn't run to another town. He obeys, and then he sits on the bank and refuses food, turning the whole thing over to Vitthal. If the songs were his, let them drown. If they were Vitthal's, let Vitthal decide. Days go by. And then, tradition says, the notebooks rose to the surface of the Indrayani, dry, and were carried back to him. The story goes one step further. It says the man who gave the order fell ill, and was healed only after he came to Tukaram, and became his follower. The tradition doesn't tell this as a victory over an enemy. It tells it as two people both being changed by the songs. Whatever happened at that river, the songs did not drown. Varkaris still sing Tukaram's abhangs. And in the season of the great walking pilgrimage to Pandharpur, a palanquin carrying his sandals sets out from Dehu, and the pilgrims walking with it sing his words along the road. A man let go of everything he'd written. The singing went on anyway.
screen: `ABHANGS, IN THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.` · `SINK THEM IN THE RIVER.` · `HE SITS AND WAITS.` · then, large: `THE NOTEBOOKS RISE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your hands rest open in your lap. Think of one thing you made or worked hard on that you're anxious about: a project, a letter, a plan, even a reputation. Picture holding it the way Tukaram held his notebooks. Now, just for this sit, imagine setting it on the water. You're not destroying it. You're only letting go of having to protect it. Breathe, and notice what it feels like to sit on the bank with empty hands. If you pray, you can leave it with God for these few minutes. The bell holds the time.
Tukaram. The grocer-saint of Dehu who sank his songs in the Indrayani when he was told to, and sat on the bank until, tradition says, they rose.
Your line: the notebooks rise. Today, when you feel the urge to defend something you made, try sitting on the bank for one breath first. Day nine hundred twenty.

921.title: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
921.hook: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
921.tomorrow: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
921.howItsDone: Kabir's dohas are sung and quoted by followers of the Kabir Panth, in Hindu devotional singing, and in everyday talk; his verses are also kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tukaram sank his notebooks in the Indrayani and sat on the bank until, tradition says, they rose. What did you stop defending? Day nine hundred twenty-one.

Before dawn, on the stone steps that run down to the Ganges at Kashi, a young weaver lies stretched across a step in the dark. He knows a famous teacher, Ramananda, comes down these steps to bathe at this hour. The teacher's foot comes down on him in the dark. Startled, Ramananda cries out the name of God: Ram, Ram. And the young man gets up and goes home, holding those words as if they'd been handed to him on purpose. That, tradition says, is how Kabir got his teacher.
screen: `STEPS DOWN TO THE GANGES.` → `A FOOT IN THE DARK.` → `RAM, RAM.`

segments.voice: Kabir is remembered as a weaver in Kashi, working a loom, raised, tradition says, by a Muslim weaver couple, Niru and Nima, who found him as a baby by a pond. A man between worlds, who spent his life making cloth and making songs. And he left a particular kind of song: the doha. A doha is a couplet, two lines that rhyme, short enough to remember after hearing it once, sharp enough to keep working on you afterward. Kabir's dohas are passed along by people singing them and quoting them. Our title promises a doha a day, so we'll take them one at a time, slowly. Here's today's. It begins, in Hindi, bura jo dekhan main chala. In English, roughly: I went out looking for the bad one, and I couldn't find anyone. Then I searched my own heart, and found no one worse than me. Two lines. Notice the trick in them. The first line starts out on a hunt, a familiar one. Who's the problem in this office, this family, this group chat? The doha lets you go out looking, and then says, flatly: found nobody. And the second line turns the lamp around. It doesn't say you're terrible. It says the search only works in one direction, inward, and that's where the material is. This is Kabir's way. He doesn't argue. He sets a little trap in two lines, and the listener walks into it and springs it. Later, when the hunt for someone to blame starts up again, the second line can come back by itself. That's what a doha is for.
screen: `A WEAVER OF KASHI.` · `THE DOHA: TWO LINES THAT RHYME.` · `I WENT LOOKING FOR THE BAD ONE.` · then, large: `I SEARCHED MY OWN HEART.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one person you've been quietly blaming lately, for a mess, a mood, a delay. Let the case against them come up, as it usually does. Then, gently, without any punishment, turn the lamp around. Ask: what did I bring to this? Not to take all the blame, just to see your own part as clearly as you saw theirs. Stay with whatever you find, without arguing. If you pray, you can hold what you found before God. The bell holds the time.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi whose dohas, two rhyming lines, set little traps. Today's: I went looking for the bad one, and searched my own heart.
Your line: I searched my own heart. Today, the next time you start the hunt for who's to blame, let the second line come back: I searched my own heart. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

922.title: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
922.hook: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
922.tomorrow: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
922.howItsDone: This doha of Kabir is quoted in Hindi homes and classrooms as a saying about love and learning, and is sung in devotional settings by those who keep Kabir's songs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's first doha: I went looking for the bad one, found no one, then searched my own heart. When did the hunt for someone to blame start up, and did the second line come back? Day nine hundred twenty-two.

A shelf sags under the weight of books. Commentaries on commentaries. A scholar has spent his life there, and he can quote line and verse on anything you ask. Down the lane, a weaver sits at a loom, throwing the shuttle back and forth. Tradition says he never learned to read. He has a two-line answer for the man with the shelf. The answer is about how much reading it takes to become wise. His count is very small.
screen: `A SHELF OF BOOKS.` → `A WEAVER AT HIS LOOM.` → `A VERY SMALL COUNT.`

segments.voice: Today's doha begins, in Hindi, pothi padh padh jag mua. A pothi is a book, a sacred text, and the line says, roughly: reading book after book, the whole world died, and not one of them became a pandit, a truly learned one. Then the second line: whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit. Two and a half letters. That's the doha's own count, and one common reading makes it a joke you can see on the page. The Hindi word for love, prem, is written with a half letter joined to the front of a full one, and then one more. Two and a half. So the whole curriculum, all the learning the scholar spent his life on, fits in a word you can write with a pencil in a second and spend a lifetime learning to read. Listen to how Kabir builds it. He doesn't say books are bad. He's a man whose verses ended up in books himself. He says something narrower and sharper: reading alone doesn't finish anyone. You can read about love until you die, and never once read love itself, the way it's written in a face, in a neighbor's need, in God. And here's the trap, the way yesterday's doha had one. Some readers stop at the first line, pleased: ha, all those books. But the second line gives you homework too. Have you read the two and a half letters? Not heard of them. Read them. In Kabir's picture, love is the text, and every day is the exam, and the exam isn't on paper.
screen: `READING BOOK AFTER BOOK.` · `NOT ONE BECAME A PANDIT.` · `TWO AND A HALF LETTERS.` · then, large: `WHOEVER READS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind one person whose love you've had to learn to read, someone who shows it badly, sideways, or in a language you didn't speak at first: a grandparent who fed you instead of talking, a friend who teases, a parent who worries out loud. Picture the way they actually show it. Read it, slowly, letter by letter, the way you'd read something precious. If you pray, you can hold that person before God, and thank God for them in whatever words you already use. The bell holds the time.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi. Today's doha: reading book after book, no one became wise; whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit.
Your line: two and a half letters. Today, read one person's love the way they actually write it, not the way you wish they would. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

923.title: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
923.hook: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
923.carry: the musk is in the deer
923.tomorrow: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)
923.howItsDone: The musk deer doha is quoted as a saying about looking for God far away, and the story of the flowers under Kabir's sheet is told by people of more than one community who honor him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's second doha: reading book after book, no one became wise, but whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit. Whose love did you read today? Day nine hundred twenty-three.

A deer is moving through the forest, head low, nose working. There's a scent in the air, rich and sweet, and it's maddening, because it's everywhere and nowhere. The deer checks behind a tree. Under a bush. Down by the stream. The scent is just as strong in each place, and never any closer. It keeps searching until it's worn out. Kabir put this deer in two lines. It's our third doha, and our last day with the weaver of Kashi.
screen: `A SCENT IN THE FOREST.` → `EVERYWHERE AND NOWHERE.` → `THE DEER KEEPS SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: The doha begins, in Hindi, kasturi kundal basai. Kasturi is musk, the prized scent. In English, roughly: the musk lives in the deer's own navel, and the deer goes searching for it through the forest. Then the second line: just so, Ram is in every body, every heart, and the world doesn't see. The joke is gentle, and the deer stands for anyone who searches. The scent was never out there. It was coming from the one doing the searching. Every place smelled of musk because the deer brought it to every place. Notice what Ram means in Kabir's mouth. It's the name his teacher cried out on the steps at Kashi. But Kabir's Ram isn't held in one temple or one image. In this doha, Ram is in every heart, and the trouble is only that we look everywhere else first. So put the three dohas together. Day one: go looking for the bad one, and you end up searching your own heart. Day two: read book after book, and still the lesson is two and a half letters, love. Day three: search the whole forest for God, and the scent was in you all along. Three hunts, and each one turns back toward the hunter. Kabir's life ends, tradition says, with one more turn. When he died, two groups of his followers, Hindus and Muslims, each wanted to give him their own last rites. Some say they argued over the body. When they lifted the sheet, there was no body there at all, only a heap of flowers. So each group took half the flowers, and honored him in its own way.
screen: `THE MUSK IS IN THE DEER.` · `RAM IN EVERY HEART.` · `THREE HUNTS, TURNED BACK.` · then, large: `ONLY FLOWERS UNDER THE SHEET.`

segments.voice: Sit still, and let the searching part of you rest. Notice the breath coming in and going out, without going anywhere to get it. It's already here. If your mind runs off into the forest, after a plan, a worry, a thing you want, that's fine; notice it, the way you'd notice the deer, and come back to the breath. Nothing to find. Just staying with what's already here, the way the musk was already in the deer. If you pray, you can rest in God as near as your own breath. The bell holds the time.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi. Today's doha: the musk is in the deer's own navel, and it searches the forest; Ram is in every heart, and the world doesn't see.
Your line: the musk is in the deer. Today, when you catch yourself hunting for something outside, check first whether the scent is coming from you. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

924.howItsDone: Hindus who love Ram read and sing the Ramcharitmanas at home and in temples, sometimes all the way through over several days, and its verses are chanted and staged in Ram Lila performances.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's last doha: the musk is in the deer, and Ram is in every heart. Where did you stop hunting and find it already near? Day nine hundred twenty-four.

It's night, and the river is high from the rains. A young man has come home to find his wife gone to her parents' house across the water, and he can't stand to wait until morning. So he crosses the swollen river, in the dark, and climbs up to her window. She is not charmed. She's embarrassed, and she tells him so, sharply. If you loved Ram, she says, the way you love this body of flesh and bone, you'd be free. The young man goes away and doesn't come back. That's how tradition tells the turning of Tulsidas.
screen: `A SWOLLEN RIVER AT NIGHT.` → `HIS WIFE'S SHARP WORDS.` → `HE TURNS TO RAM.`

segments.voice: Tulsidas became a poet of Ram, and his great work is the Ramcharitmanas, the story of Ram retold in Awadhi, a language people spoke, not the Sanskrit of the older Ramayana. For the next three days we'll stay with him, starting at the poem's front door. The Manas opens with a short run of Sanskrit verses, as if Tulsidas bows at the threshold in the old language before stepping inside in the new one. The very first verse bows to Vani, the goddess of speech, and to Vinayaka, Ganesha: makers of letters and meanings, of the flavors and meters of verse, and of everything auspicious. A poet, before writing a word, thanks the one who gives words, and the one who clears the road. Then comes a line that's easy to miss. Tulsidas says why he is writing: for the happiness of his own heart, svantah sukhaya. Not for fame. He tells the story of Ram because telling it makes him glad. And the poem explains its own name. It says Shiva composed this story first and kept it in his own mind, his manas, and so it's called the Manas of Ram's deeds. Tulsidas, in other words, says he's passing on something Shiva has been holding in his heart. Now look back at this week. Namdev and a dog and a turning temple. Tukaram's split sugarcane, and his notebooks rising from the river. Kabir's three dohas, each turning the hunt back on the hunter. And Tulsidas, turned around by his wife's sharp words, sitting down to write for the joy of it.
screen: `THE MANAS, IN AWADHI.` · `A BOW TO VANI AND VINAYAKA.` · `FOR MY OWN HEART'S JOY.` · then, large: `KEPT IN SHIVA'S MIND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath settle. Think of one thing you do, or used to do, simply because it makes you glad: singing in the car, drawing, cooking, telling a story to a child. Not for anyone's praise, not to prove anything. Let it come back to you with its sound and its feel. Notice what happens inside you when you remember it. Then, the way Tulsidas bowed before he started, let yourself be thankful for whatever gave you that gift. If you pray, you can offer that thanks to God. The bell holds the time.
Tulsidas. The poet of the Ramcharitmanas, who bowed to Vani and Vinayaka at its door, and wrote the story of Ram for the happiness of his own heart.
Your line: for my own heart's joy. Today, do one small thing for the joy of it, svantah sukhaya. Day nine hundred twenty-four.
